assessment.nobel_worthiness: Flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform for correlated insulators, superconductivity and ferromagnetism in a single tunable material. It is a clean case of a calculation predicting a striking quantum behaviour that experiment then realised, and it created the field of moire quantum materials. As a condensed-matter theorist this is the kind of discovery I find most compelling.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the continuum-model prediction of the magic angle in 2011, and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 observation of correlated insulating states and superconductivity. Prediction plus experiment gives a natural, fair configuration within three names. Experimental credit is shared with co-authors such as Yuan Cao and others who are not on this list, and the allocation between the first-author student and the group leader is a normal but real question.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups have reproduced the correlated phases and extended them to twisted multilayers and other moire systems. The field is highly active, and the basic picture of the flat bands is stable. Recognition is arguably timely, though the nature of the superconducting pairing is still debated.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is not settled.
Sample-to-sample variation and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility of the finer details.
Early related theory by others (e.g. Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) may need weighing; I cannot verify the exact priority from the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall effects revealed a new class of electronic states with protected edge and surface transport, grounded in band-structure topology. The work is original, conceptually clear and has had a broad impact on materials physics and on ideas for dissipationless electronics and topological qubits.
assessment.attribution: Kane provided the central theory of the Z2 topological insulator (with Mele, who is not in this entry). Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental quantum spin Hall observation in HgTe, and Xue's group the first quantum anomalous Hall effect. This is a reasonable three-person set, although it leaves out Mele, Bernevig, Zhang and Hasan, so the allocation is sensitive to how the theory is divided. The 2016 prize to Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz covered related topological ideas, which complicates the distinction.
assessment.maturity: The effects are confirmed independently in several material families and the interpretation is stable. The quantum anomalous Hall effect is measured to high precision. The topic is mature enough for recognition, with the main risk being overlap with the 2016 prize.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as distinct enough from the 2016 topological-phases prize.
Priority and credit between Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu-Kane-Mele is contested.
Practical impact in devices remains limited so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmions are topologically protected spin textures that were first observed as a lattice in chiral magnets and later as individual objects in thin films and at interfaces. They tie directly to my own field of magnetism and spin dynamics, and they link a clear theoretical concept to measurement by neutron scattering, Lorentz microscopy and spin-polarised STM.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer's group found the skyrmion lattice in MnSi (with Boni and collaborators), Wiesendanger's group showed single atomic-scale skyrmions at an interface, and Tokura's group did real-space imaging and room-temperature materials. The theoretical foundation by Bogdanov and others is not credited in this entry, which is an important gap. The configuration is workable but the omission of the theory pioneers is a concern.
assessment.maturity: Skyrmions are confirmed by many groups in many materials and by several complementary probes. The device-level promise (racetrack memory) has been slow to materialise, but the discovery itself is well established.
uncertainties: Credit for the theoretical prediction (Bogdanov and colleagues) is not represented among the credited names.
Technological relevance is still unproven.
Who among the experimental groups was decisive is debatable, and Tokura is also credited elsewhere in other entries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Giant room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and especially the coherent-tunnelling MgO junctions, underlies read heads and magnetic random-access memory. The physics is spin-dependent tunnelling and symmetry filtering of Bloch states, which is well described by first-principles calculation, a point that appeals to me. It is a natural successor to the 2007 GMR prize.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported room-temperature TMR in 1995, and Yuasa (and Parkin's group, who are not credited here) demonstrated large MgO-based TMR in 2004. The theory of coherent tunnelling by Butler and Mathon is not included. A three-person prize would be defensible but it excludes some decisive contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature, commercially deployed for years, independently confirmed. Recognition would be timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Parkin and the first-principles theorists (Butler, Mathon) are missing from the credited names.
The 2007 prize may be seen as having covered much of the spintronics territory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spin-orbit torques allow electrical current to switch magnetisation through spin-orbit coupling without a spin-polarised source, in heavy-metal and ferromagnet bilayers. This is a rich piece of magnetism physics (Rashba-Edelstein and spin Hall mechanisms) with a clear route to fast, low-power memory. It interests me for the interplay of theory, spin dynamics and device use.
assessment.attribution: Miron and Gambardella reported current-induced switching in a Pt/Co/AlOx structure in 2010-2011, while Buhrman's group demonstrated spin-Hall-driven switching in 2012. Which mechanism is dominant, and the credit between the spin Hall and Rashba routes, is a real question. Theory contributors and early spin-Hall researchers are not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced and being developed in industry, but the microscopic origin is still discussed in some systems, so the physical picture is less settled than for TMR.
uncertainties: Relative importance of bulk spin Hall and interfacial Rashba contributions is not fully resolved.
Credit relative to the spin Hall effect pioneers is unclear.
Technology adoption is still maturing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gives a controlled, non-perturbative way to treat strong electron correlation and was the first scheme to capture the Mott transition with both Hubbard bands and a quasiparticle peak. Combined with DFT it is now a standard tool for correlated materials. As a first-principles theorist I know its value in practice, though a methods prize is a harder sell than a discovery.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar developed the mapping to an impurity problem, and Kotliar and others built LDA+DMFT. Walter Metzner is not credited here, and the split of credit is a real concern. The three given names are a reasonable but incomplete grouping.
assessment.maturity: Decades of use and independent validation, including in cold-atom simulators. The method is mature, but the quantitative accuracy for real materials is mixed.
uncertainties: Omission of Metzner and others who founded the large-dimension limit.
The committee may prefer a physical discovery to a theoretical method.
Reliability of DMFT for quantitative predictions in real materials varies.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model and the superfluid-Mott insulator transition in a controlled setting, with single-site imaging by quantum gas microscopes. It lets many-body theory be tested directly, which is a strong link between calculation and experiment.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch (with Cirac, Gardiner) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch with Hansch carried out the 2002 Mott transition experiment, and Bloch and Greiner developed microscopes. Jaksch is not credited, and the line to the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize is something to weigh. A three-name subset of Bloch, Greiner and Zoller seems a reasonable choice, with Cirac omitted.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely replicated. Fermi-Hubbard physics in the regime of real interest, such as d-wave pairing, has not been reached, so the open question remains whether the biggest scientific payoff has yet come.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier cold-atom prizes.
Credit among the theory proposers (Zoller, Cirac, Jaksch) is unresolved.
Whether it has yielded a decisive new physical result beyond demonstrating the platform.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third basic class of collinear magnetic order, with zero net magnetisation but spin-split bands, derived from symmetry and first-principles calculation. If it holds up broadly, it is a conceptual advance in magnetism and a notable example of theory plus electronic-structure calculation leading experiment. This falls squarely within my field.
assessment.attribution: Smejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth formulated the classification and the unifying symmetry framework in 2022, building on earlier work by Hayami, Yanagi, Kusunose and others, and on earlier ideas in the spin-split antiferromagnet literature. The priority questions relative to those Japanese groups and others are real, so the credit allocation is not yet clear.
assessment.maturity: It is recent. ARPES and other spectroscopy have confirmed spin splitting in MnTe and CrSb, but the field is only a few years old, and I regard recognition now as likely premature in a field I know well.
uncertainties: Priority relative to Hayami, Yanagi and Kusunose and other earlier work.
Experimental confirmation is limited to a few materials and techniques so far.
Technological significance is not yet shown.
